subject: Agriculture
title: The Three Sisters
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Three Sisters.

hook.text: Indigenous Americans grew corn, beans, and squash together in the same mound. They called them the Three Sisters.

buildup.text: Corn grows tall and provides a pole. Beans climb the stalk and fix nitrogen in the soil.

discovery.text: Squash spreads along the ground, shading out weeds and keeping the soil moist with its broad leaves.

twist.text: Together, they form a complete protein and a self-fertilizing ecosystem. Separately, each is less productive.

climax.text: This companion planting system sustained civilizations across the Americas for thousands of years.

punchline.text: Three crops, one mound—nature's perfect team.

quiz.question: What role do beans play in the Three Sisters companion planting?
options: Climb the corn stalk and fix nitrogen

details.summary: The Three Sisters—corn, beans, and squash—were grown together by Indigenous peoples of the Americas as a complementary agricultural system. This topic covers the agronomic genius of this intercropping method and its cultural significance to Native American communities.
details.whyItMatters: The Three Sisters system is one of the most elegant examples of sustainable agriculture in history, providing a nutritionally complete diet from three mutually supporting crops grown together.
takeaways: Corn provides a climbing structure for beans; beans fix nitrogen for all three crops
Squash leaves shade the soil, suppressing weeds and retaining moisture
Together, the three crops provide a nutritionally balanced diet of carbs, protein, and vitamins

faq.question: How does the Three Sisters planting system work?
faq.answer: Corn grows tall as a pole for beans to climb. Beans fix atmospheric nitrogen that fertilizes all three crops. Squash spreads along the ground, shading soil to suppress weeds and retain moisture. Together they outperform monocultures.

faq.question: What is the cultural importance of the Three Sisters?
faq.answer: Many Native American nations consider the Three Sisters sacred gifts that sustain both body and spirit. The crops feature prominently in creation stories, ceremonies, and food traditions, representing interdependence and community sustenance.
